title: Clandestine Love Career and Wedded Course
paragraphs: Tolkāppiyam shows us that
Karaṇam (marriage) is The hero taking the heroine’s hand in marriage As she is offered by those of a line worthy and compatible With the rites and ceremonies attendant thereon.
He also shows that It is marriage As the lovers take to elopement Without the heroine’s parents offering her hand.
In both the events The lovers enter into wedded course
And make a blissful living to the acclaim of the world.
The order of Tolkāppiyar’s day was that The hero stood on a higher plane In the domestic sphere and in other realms of activity too.
Being so, In this flower-garden of Tolkāppiyam that I write, I make no attempt whatever to change that order.
Tolkāppiyar steers clear of any controversy With regard to God or religion he believed in And holds forth God and religion universal.
Such is the way Aiyaṉ Tiruvaḷḷuvar has chosen later, Keeping religion and God secular.
The Akam lovers are seen running their household In tune with the norms of both Tolkāppiyar and Tiruvaḷḷuvar.
The bud called clandestine love course Blossoms into the flower called wedded course By marriage.

Malivu the ecstasy of union of the lovers, Pulavi the feigned reserve of the heroine, Ūṭal the sulking of the lovers leading to sexual fulfilment, Uṇarvu the resolution of sulking through the interceders, And pirivu the separation occasioned by the parting of the hero In quest of wealth and learning And for acts of valour for the country’s good -- Occur during the wedded course after marriage.

“O my manna pure! Honey unsatiating! Do tell me without concealing. During those days of our clandestine career, When we were showering love unexhausted on each other, Why did you try to draw my heart apart And drown it in the flood of devotion to God?”
Queried the hero.

“It was my confidante’s counsel That we should worship and adore God For our love to come to fruition without hassles. But are you angry about it now?” So saying the heroine served food on his leaf plate And sat by him to eat together with him.
“How is it that The food turns manna with your hand’s touch? Not just that. The flower too acquires a new fragrance! Are all these because of the bliss of God?” Wondered the hero.
“It is all because my God dwells in my heart.”
As she said thus, Both of them forgot the food cooked and served on the plate, Vied with each other And relished the lips of each other.
Food taken They commented: “There is one thing that tastes sweet; It is not the manna but the lips!”

Since it was the early days of wedded life They made no distinction As to whether it was morning, noon or evening Or day or night, And realized their dreams of passion Which they yearned for in their clandestine course.
Realizing that He who lives a virtuous life is known as a brahmin, They decided by the dictates of their wisdom And followd the path of domestic virtue.

But the dreams of their furtive career refused to die down! They went about recalling in joy those days When many a hurdle ran into their way Which they overcame using many a strategy And when their companions came to their aid unfailing. And they glossed over things unsavoury too When there intervened the beat of the drum called sulking.
“One day I stood waiting there for you Till my legs threatened to break And you did not turn up!”
The hero said in response quick: “None too good were you too! Another day I waited for you sleepless through the night And you failed to turn up!”
All these accusations mutual Amounted at length to letters written on the air!
The interceders stepping in, The false sullen mood Gave way to the bliss of joy ensuing. Should we need to tell those versed in this art That sulking adds to the joy of union?

> [Thirty-three are the contexts structured > That find the hero of ineffable note > Marking his utterances:] > > When union occasions with the heroine > After they have come through the marriage solemnized, > A union freed of all reticence and reserve; > > As he stays immersed in the joy of union unbounded; > As there mainfests an awesome wifely rectitude in the heroine;

> As they meet the charges of household > Guided by the worthy tradition of the old; > > As he weighs the days of disquiet of the furtive course > Against the abiding bliss of this wedded state; > > As the confidante adores the guardian deity > That stood them in good stead in days of adversity; > > As the heroine speaks now with passion’s fervour > With the days of care and distress withered away; > > As he wonders, > While taking food and wearing garlands, > How things taste sweet as ambrosia to him > When they pass through her hands; > > As he commends to her > Courtesies due to > Sages, learned men and others of exemplary conduct; > > As he addresses his heart > Reminiscing in a sorrowing mood > About those days of the clandestine-course > When they had union scarce and far between; > > As they revel in the bliss of wedded union > With the hardships and rigours of the clandestine course > Vanishing like letters inscribed on the air; > > As he comes forth with words of reassurance > ‘Go not dispirited’ and ‘Fear not the hardship of my journey;’ > > As there occurs the breach of his promise thereof; > > As he finds the heroine - > The one embodying fortitude and lofty bearing > And with discerning maids-in-attendance... . > > (Poruḷatikāram : Karpiyal, verse 5)
